To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

persistent nocturnal hypertension, as defined by a nocturnal blood pressure level above 120% of daytime level, and non-dipping pattern of blood pressure during nocturnal sleep, defined as a decrease in blood pressure below 10% during sleep, are strongly and independently associated with increased cardiovascular and renal morbidity and mortality.
nocturnal hypertension and the non-dipping blood-pressure pattern are associated with increased risk for cardiovascular disease and renal damage.
persistent nocturnal hypertension is a strong predictor of cardiovascular risk and that non-dipping of nocturnal blood pressure is an independent predictor of cardiovascular events.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how nocturnal and non-dipping patterns of hypertension may contribute to the development of adverse cardiovascular and renal outcomes.
the role of nocturnal hypertension and the non-dipping pattern of blood pressure during the night in the development of cardiovascular disease.
understanding how the circadian clock regulates the expression of genes that control blood pressure, the renin angiotensin system and renal function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
persistent nocturnal hypertension is a risk marker of adverse cardiovascular and renal outcomes.
nocturnal hypertension and/or non-dipping of the blood pressure pattern is associated with increased risk for future cardiovascular events and death.

nocturnal hypertension, non-dipping blood pattern, and abnormal circadian blood pressure pattern are all associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events and renal damage, but whether this is a direct cause-and-effect relationship remains uncertain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nocturnal hypertension and nocturnal non-dipping of the blood pressure pattern are associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events.
nocturnal hypertension and nocturnal non-dipping are independent predictors of poor cardiovascular outcomes.
nocturnal hypertension and/or non-dipping blood pressures are independent predictors of adverse cardiovascular and renal outcomes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
nocturnal hypertension and nocturnal dipping are distinct clinical entities that may be associated with different pathophysiological mechanisms and cardiovascular risk.
nocturnal hypertension and/or non-dipping blood pressures, as opposed to daytime hypertension alone, may be a better indicator of cardiovascular risk and may be a useful therapeutic target.
nocturnal blood pressure is an important determinant of cardiovascular and renal outcomes.
